stories.title: Lessons for the BJP from Uttar Pradesh MLC election
stories.summary: The first big takeaway for the BJP is that the results of the MLC election demonstrate the 2024 Lok Sabha results may not be a fluke, when the SP, with 37 seats, brought down the BJP’s handsome tallies of 71 seats in 2014 and 62 seats in 2019 to 33 seats in 2024

article_sentences: The results of the Uttar Pradesh MLC (Members of Legislative Council) election for 11 seats, including both the Graduates’ and Teachers’ constituencies, has left much food for thought for the State BJP going into an Assembly election early next year, not least because the party may have to jettison more than half of its sitting MLAs going ahead.
While the BJP bagged six out of the 11 seats in the fray and has done better than its rival, the Samajwadi Party (SP), within this meta narrative, however, are worries for the BJP.

stories.headline: Year 2026 resembles 1991, could be deemed as inflection point for Indian economy: Chief Economic Advisor
stories.title: Year 2026 resembles 1991, could be deemed as inflection point for Indian economy: Chief Economic Advisor
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 29: The year 2026 resembles 1991, and it could be deemed an inflection point for the Indian economy, which has been facing not only external challenges but also structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology, Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran said on Thursday. Addressing the ISID-IDRA national conference, Nageswaran further said that, in the global context, India is a source of macroeconomic stability and resilience, which sometimes tend to get forgotten in the noisy world of social media narratives. “2026 resembles 1991, and many of you should not immediately think that when we talk about the word resemblance, it is not the same as identical. Identical means that you have the same balance of payments crisis. “No. The point is, it was an inflection point for us in 1991, and 2026 is also, or even 2025, could be deemed as inflection points for us,” he said. Nageswaran said that while the 1991 balance of crisis brought four decades of accumulated constraints to a head- a moment of reckoning more than a passing shock- the external stress of 2026 has brought India to a fork in its growth journey and invites a fundamental re-examination of strategy. “In 2026, the challenge is not only external. Structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology add to the pressure,” he said. Nageswaran pointed out that the worst shocks now arrive not because of accidents of nature, but by design. “Just as last week, we saw China announcing an export licensing regime for tunnel boring machines and for many other products of infrastructure goods, which India will be needing,” he said. The CEA said the weaponised dependence ends up eroding the more they are used, that is true. “The more countries weaponise their supplies, they become less effective over time. But there is a period when they are binding, because other countries cannot ramp up production just like that,” he said. Nageswaran observed that the next 20-30 years will be different from the 40 years pre-pandemic and added that most of the shocks which we faced before the pandemic were largely demand deficiency shocks. “So central bankers and fiscal policy could just stimulate and try to get out of trouble, whether it is the 1987 stock market crash, 1990-91 savings and loan crisis, the East Asian crisis of 1997–98, 2001 tech bubble or the 2008 global financial crisis. “Every single crisis was met with a standard playbook of low interest rates, together with or without quantitative easing, and some fiscal stimulus as well,” he said. The CEA said it is easy to stimulate when you consider the problems as only a matter of demand deficiency, but when supply falls short, it is about real stuff. “And that is not easily engineered or designed by monetary or fiscal policy. And higher interest rates, you can raise rates sky-high and cool an overheated economy,” he said. Nageswaran said in the next 30 years, monetary policy will be much more difficult to execute in a world of supply shortages causing real economic disruptions, both to output and to inflation. “Fiscal policy, broad support, stimulating of the economy where animal spirits are weak; it is easy to stimulate them with fiscal stimulus,” he said.

stories.headline: Stop sermonising others; introspect why BJP lost Varanasi seats in MLC polls: Congress slams PM
stories.title: Stop sermonising others; introspect why BJP lost Varanasi seats in MLC polls: Congress slams PM
stories.summary: New Deli, Oct 29: The Congress on Thursday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his taunt at the opposition party’s showing in the MLC elections, saying he must stop trolling and sermonising others and instead reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi. Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said that from Varanasi and Nagpur to Lucknow, Prayagraj, and Patna, the people have clearly passed a “no-confidence motion against” the PM’s policies. “The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he’s sermonising others! Before counting Congress’s seats, I wish he’d also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS’s stronghold of Nagpur?” Ramesh said in his post in Hindi on X. “Modi, stop the trolling. Crores of families are reeling from back-breaking inflation, the youth are unemployed, and private investment has ground to a halt,” he said. Drop the arrogance and reflect on these issues, Ramesh said. “From Varanasi and Nagpur to Lucknow, Prayagraj, and Patna, the people have clearly passed a no-confidence motion against your policies,” the Congress leader said. The Congress on Wednesday had hit back at Prime Minister Modi over his taunt, saying that if the PM is so confident that EVMs have no bearing on election results, he should prove his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess through action, not rhetoric. The Congress said if the PM believes that EVMs have no bearing on the election results then he should commit to conducting all Lok Sabha and upcoming Vidhan Sabha elections by ballot paper, going forward. The opposition party’s assertion came after Prime Minister Modi taunted the Congress for its dismal show in the MLC elections despite the use of paper ballots, a key demand of opposition parties in their campaign against EVMs. The BJP and its NDA allies won 16 of the 28 seats in the legislative council elections held across four states as the Congress won one, while the Samajwadi Party emerged winner in five seats in Uttar Pradesh, including two in Varanasi.

stories.headline: HC strikes down water usage charges on hydel projects
stories.title: HC strikes down water usage charges on hydel projects
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 29: In a significant decision, the High Court of J&K and Ladakh Thursday struck down the levy of water usage charges on hydropower projects under the Jammu and Kashmir Water Resources (Regulation and Management) Act, 2010. In response to independent power producers’ pleas, which it allowed finally, a Division Bench of Justice Sanjay Dhar and Justice Rajnesh Oswal declared the Act of 2010 ultra vires the constitution to extent it imposed water usage charges upon the aggrieved companies and struck it down to that extent. The court noted that the charges effectively amounted to a tax on electricity generation that the erstwhile state legislature was not competent to impose, even as it restrained the government from imposing any tax on the generation of electricity under the “garb of water usage charges or any other tax.” Eleven independent power producers (IPPs) had petitioned court through their counsel, Shariq J Reyaz while two others had approached it through senior advocate Pranav Kohli, challenging the levy of charges for the use of water in generating hydroelectricity. The companies had questioned the legality of the charges imposed under the 2010 Act, contending that the use of water by hydropower projects was non-consumptive and that the levy, in substance, amounted to a tax on electricity generation rather than a fee for the use of water. They had also challenged the demand notices issued by the authorities in respect of water usage charges for generation of electricity pursuant to the provisions contained in the act. Opposing the pleas, the J&K government defended the levy with the contention that water resources fell within the legislative domain of the state and that the charges were regulatory in nature. In its stand, the Union of India had maintained that the state legislature was not competent to impose a tax on electricity generation, as the relevant constitutional entry empowers states to tax the consumption or sale of electricity, but not its generation. Disagreeing with the J&K government’s stand, the court noted that the nature of a levy had to be determined by its substance and actual operation rather than the nomenclature assigned to it. The bench observed that the charges were calculated with reference to the head height from which water was used to propel turbines, rather than the quantity of water drawn or consumed. This indicated that the levy was linked to the electricity-generating potential of the water, it noted. Moreover, the court observed that the charges collected from hydropower projects were intended to fund the establishment of hydel and multipurpose hydroelectric projects, purchase of existing projects, investment in transmission and distribution networks, and procurement of electricity by the government or its entities. Since the levy was not linked to any specific service rendered to the hydropower projects, it possessed the character of a tax rather than a water usage fee, the court underscored. The erstwhile state legislature, it said, lacked the competence to impose such a tax when the legislation was enacted in 2010. “Even if it is assumed that usage charges constitute a tax on water and not a tax on generation of electricity, still then the respondent-State does not have a case to save the legislation,” the bench said, adding, “This is so because even if it is assumed that the “land” includes “water” or that water is “mineral” still then in the face of nature of categorization of various fields in entries appearing in the State List, it becomes clear that waterfalls under a separate and distinct category whereas land and minerals fall under distinct categories.” While the “water” has been categorized separately under Entry 17 of List-II, the court said, the land has been categorised separately under Entry 18 of List-II with taxing Entry 49. “Taxing entry for minerals is Entry 50 of List-II. However, there is no taxing entry in the State List in respect of the water,” the court said. It also rejected J&K government’s argument that the subsequent adoption of the Act of 2010 under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, could validate a provision that was unconstitutional at its inception. “The argument appears to be an attempt in desperation to save the impugned legislation. If we have a look at the provisions of the J&K Reorganisation Act, it becomes clear that what is being provided under the said Act is saving of certain State enactments and repeal of certain others,” the court said. It also said that the legislation also provides for extension of Central enactments to the UTs of J&K and Ladakh and adoption of State enactments.” Merely because the Act provides for adoption of State enactments and saves their application to UTs of J&K and Ladakh, the enactments do not become the enactments passed by the Parliament, the court underlined. “If we accept the said argument, it would lead to absurdities. It shall result in a situation where a subject which, as per the Reorganisation Act, is reserved for the UT of J&K for legislative and executive powers, would become a subject of the Union Government,” the court said “This is not the intention of the J&K Reorganisation Act. In fact, Section 32(1) of the said Act clearly delineates the subjects over which the UT of J&K has legislative and executive powers. Merely because the certain State Acts have been adopted in terms of the J&K Re-organisation Act, which is an enactment of the Parliament, the adopted enactments would not cease to be enactments of the State of UT of J&K.” The court concluded by declaring the relevant provisions of the 2010 Act “ultra vires” the constitution and struck them down insofar as they imposed water usage charges on the petitioners' hydropower projects.

article_sentences: - Reliance Jio recently IPOed, and by now, everyone who sold the stock after some listing gains, might be wondering, what if they held a little longer, it could have been more profits.
- But when it comes to money, Jio does not think short-term like some of the listing gain investors.
- It is not in Reliance's DNA to think short-term, and just think about money.
Reliance, and its telecom entity Jio knows how to play the long game.
That is what the company effectively did when it came up with the services in 2016 by offering free data and SIM cards, and unlimited voice calling.
But since the company is listed in the stock exchanges now, and there are thousands of shareholders, the need to focus on short-term performance improvement grows.
Jio has been noticing an increase in profit margins and overall profits quarter after quarter.
This will likely remain unchanged, until and unless the company goes on to invest a large amount of money in spectrum.
The telco’s debt is about to go down.
But as the focus shifts on the profitability and improvement, as most publicly listed companies do, the tariffs will have to go up.
While tariff hikes are very important for the telcos to boost revenues in India, Jio remains committed to be the most affordable player in the market.

“Jio has always stood for being the most affordable player in the market and giving the highest quality of services value for money, and we’ll always stand for that,” said Akash Ambani, Chairman of Jio Platforms Limited (JPL).
